shortDescription: New Zealand's High Court has struck down regulations banning new prescriptions of puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria, ruling that the measures were made unlawfully and amounted to unjustified discrimination.

children: New Zealand's High Court has struck down regulations banning new prescriptions of puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria, ruling that the measures were made unlawfully and amounted to unjustified discrimination.

Justice Dale La Hood set aside the regulations, introduced in late 2025, which barred new patients under 18 from receiving gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues for gender dysphoria or gender incongruence

La Hood, in a summary released on Wednesday, found the government had failed to meet consultation obligations under the Medicines Act because groups approached by the Ministry of Health had not been clearly told that an outright prohibition on new prescriptions was under consideration
The judge also said there was insufficient urgency to justify not consulting directly with gender-diverse young people
The decision followed a judicial review brought by the Professional Association for Transgender Health Aotearoa, or PATHA, against Health Minister Simeon Brown

The government had argued the restrictions were a precautionary response to uncertainty over the long-term benefits and risks of puberty blockers, and reflected bans on the drugs overseas, including in Britain following the landmark Cass Review into gender care for adolescents
An earlier interim court order had prevented the measures' enforcement while the challenge was heard

A spokesperson for the Health Minister said the Government was committed to introducing new safeguards on the prescribing of gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues, while ensuring patients with medical needs could continue to access appropriate care and was seeking advice on next steps
